Le mardi 3 mai 2022, à midi, un duo de m: On Tuesday, May 3, 2022, at noon, a duo of musicians opens the first Semaine jazz de Saint-Henri with an outdoor concert at Place du Bonheur-d’Occasion. A few fans are there, and curious passersby stop to enjoy the sun and the music. Jason Magellan, 18, was passing through on his way to the optometrist. He has lived in the neighbouring area, Petite-Bourgogne, since he was five. “It’s my passion,” he says of music.
Jason est un pianiste autodidacte. « Je: Jason is a self-taught pianist. “I only play at home,” he says. COVID makes things difficult. “It’s just a hobby, but I’d like to take it more seriously,” adds the young musician, who likes stride, ragtime and blues. He also likes classical music, and in high school he learned to play the trombone.
« J’ai appris le piano et à lire la musi: “I taught myself piano and how to read music. I practised and practised, and it just came together,” says Jason. His love of jazz was passed on to him by the community, in the neighbourhood that is the cradle of this music in Montréal.
Jason Megellan, musicien, à la Place du: Jason Megellan, musician, at Place du Bonheur-d'Occasion Photo: Christelle Saint-Julien
« Je n’étais pas au courant ; une chance: “I didn’t know about it; lucky I was passing by!” he exclaims of the music festival. “I think it’s really cool that they’re doing this here; the last time, I was really little,” Jason continues, recalling the last time he heard an outdoor concert in the area.
« La Petite-Bourgogne, c’est le nom gent: “Petite-Bourgogne is the gentrified name of this neighbourhood,” explains Valérie Lacombe, a musician and co-founder of the <l1>Société de Jazz de Saint-Henri,</l1> the non-profit organization behind the festival. In 1966, an urban renewal program gave the area its new name.
Jusque-là, les limites entre le quartier: Until then, the boundaries between the English-speaking working-class neighbourhood, where the city’s Black population was concentrated, and the French-speaking working-class neighbourhood of Saint-Henri were blurry. In 2019, Valérie and Sam Kirmayer founded the SJSH with a community focus. “The original idea was to offer a space other than universities to build community, exchange ideas and practise an oral tradition,” explains Valérie. The couple, both musicians, have lived in the neighbourhood for eight years. When he arrived in Saint-Henri, freshly graduated in jazz guitar and looking for a jazz community in the historic neighbourhood, Sam went to the local venues to play.
Les <em>jams </em>hebdomadaires, qui ont: The weekly jams, held in bars and restaurants in the area, became popular events in the neighbourhood.
« Des gens de différentes générations ve: “People from different generations came, which doesn’t happen often with jazz,” he says. Over the years, these jams built a community of their own. Everyone could take part. “It just proved to us that jazz is a music that can bring people together. It’s a powerful music that lets people be themselves, and be together,” says Valérie.
Sam Kirmayer et Valérie Lacombe. Photo:: Sam Kirmayer and Valérie Lacombe. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
Puis, la pandémie frappe, et l’idée de c: Then the pandemic hit, and the idea of creating a festival celebrating jazz and community – in the very place where this music comes from – took root. Within four months, after securing the necessary funding, the five members of the board of directors set to work with determination to organize the Semaine jazz de Saint-Henri. They first had to make sure they had the financial resources before launching. “We’re fed up with artists and musicians, like jazz musicians, not being paid decently,” says Sam. The organization, made up exclusively of volunteers, put everything together in a few weeks: some twenty events, including concerts, listening sessions, master classes and discussions, are scheduled over six days. The goal is to strengthen the community through jazz. The musicians are hired, everything is planned.
Le dimanche 8 mai à 23 h, le festival ti: On Sunday, May 8, at 11 p.m., the festival winds down in an electric atmosphere. The five board members – Valérie Lacombe, Sam Kirmayer, Carolina Guevara, Ariane Perreault and Mark Dawson – take a moment to take stock. The team has just spent the previous six days wearing every hat on the ground to make sure the Semaine jazz de Saint-Henri ran smoothly, and several months planning the activities.
Tous les billets de chacun des événement: Every ticket for every event sold out, and the venues were filled to capacity at each performance. “People came,” says Ariane Perreault, the communications manager, delighted. No one could have predicted that the concerts would end up selling out. The non-profit couldn’t count on the services of a publicist for the festival: the budget was tight, and the timeline even tighter. “We’ve been working for a long time and couldn’t see the results,” adds Ariane.
Maintenant, on peut aussi voir ce que ça: “Now, we can also see what it can become.” What struck her most were all the curious people who came to have a first experience of jazz, says the woman who once lived in Saint-Henri and now works there. Her love of the neighbourhood is one of the reasons she decided to join the project. “When I moved here, my father told me about the history of the neighbourhood, and the Black communities who arrived here; it’s something I had never heard about,” she recalls. The last time Carolina Guevara, project coordinator at the SJSH, went to the Festival International de Jazz de Montréal, she didn’t enjoy the experience. “Today’s Jazz Festival is about commercial interests,” says the urban planner by trade, who is finishing a master’s degree in the field.
Ça m’a fait penser à la façon dont la vi: It made me think about how the city invested in transforming the Place des Arts, mainly for that event.” “Does that mean it’s a city’s musicians who keep jazz alive, or is it the places, or the lack of places, that dictate where jazz is lived?” asks Carolina. She pushes the reflection even further. “How superficial is the jazz label? How is it that, even with fantastic musicians and schools, we don’t hear more jazz, or hear more talk about jazz?” As circumstances would have it, rather than writing an academic paper on the subject, she joined the SJSH board of directors and now devotes herself to organizing the festival with the rest of the team.
Selon elle, ce type d’événement est esse: In her view, this type of event is essential in a city. “It’s necessary to have this kind of activity in order to create places and to associate these activities with a community of people who can contribute to them and shape the collective imagination,” says the coordinator.
Mark Dawson, directeur artistique de la: Mark Dawson, artistic director of the SJSH, has been able to observe these connections between music and social life up close. “It’s not just about jazz, or Saint-Henri, or the community, but about much more: all of these things at once, and where they meet,” he says.
Caroline Guevara et Mark Dawson, à l'org: Caroline Guevara and Mark Dawson, festival organizers. Photo: Pierre Langlois
Valérie Lacombe, la cofondatrice du fest: Valérie Lacombe, the festival’s co-founder, believes above all that people first connected through an interest in the musical performance, and then through the power of music. “Live music has the power to bring people together,” she says.
Dans le cadre de la Semaine jazz de Sain: As part of the Semaine jazz de Saint-Henri, three New York headliners – Jeremy Pelt, saxophonist Nicole Glover and drummer Billy Drummond – will share the stage each day starting at 7 p.m. In the jazz tradition, they will be joined by local and American musicians playing in groups assembled for a handful of concerts.
Ces prestations seront suivies d’un seco: These performances will be followed by a second concert by local musicians, then a jam, the kind of musical circle anyone can join. “You’re going to see me play!” says Jason. For the past few weeks, the new venue Basement has regularly been turning into a neighbourhood jazz club. During the festival, the mood inside its walls is festive. You feel transported to another era in the dimly lit room, with an attentive audience and musicians feeding the atmosphere. The line for the free concerts stretches down the street. The jam goes on until the wee hours of the morning, as if nothing else mattered.
À la soirée inaugurale de la Semaine jaz: At the Semaine jazz’s opening night, Jason is in the audience. The young musician will be one of the last to leave the festival that evening. He meets the musicians and the team. At the jam, a musician from Ottawa gives him an impromptu theory lesson. “It was so much fun, I loved it, I’m coming back tomorrow,” he says. “We created all of this for him,” says Valérie Lacombe with gratitude. While the young man happened to be there by chance, it will take redoubled efforts to bring in young people from the neighbourhood and to have Black communities gather there.
L’un des objectifs de la SJSH est de met: One of the SJSH’s goals is to make a place available to everyone. “The goal is to create a space where people can meet, have a creative space, but also a place where they can simply come. I want people to feel that there’s a space for them,” says Valérie.
Cette invitation s’adresse tout particul: This invitation is aimed especially at local youth, particularly those who have traditionally been excluded from music institutions. “I want them to know they can come and see the best musicians, and see people their own age play, and that they can talk to them.”
Il s’agit de quelque chose à développer: This is something to develop in the future, to make it truly accessible to those they want to serve. There is a lot of work ahead! “And also, [we need] more Black people in positions of power,” she says, bringing us back to the origins and history of this music, issues that, unfortunately, are often forgotten.
Le bassiste montréalais Leighton Harrel,: Montréal bassist Leighton Harrel, in concert. Photo: Pierre Langlois
Au quotidien, Jason sent-il l’esprit du: In everyday life, does Jason feel the spirit of jazz in his neighbourhood? “People don’t respect the neighbourhood’s idols enough, despite the murals,” the young man believes. “The park is called Oscar-Peterson, but people still call it Campbell. Sometimes people ask who’s in the picture,” he says of the murals that adorn the neighbourhood’s walls. While the neighbourhood’s elders know the history, Jason wishes it were passed on more to his generation. “I was introduced to jazz by Michael Farkas.
Grâce à lui j’ai rencontré Oliver Jones: Thanks to him I met Oliver Jones,” he continues. The jazz legend, born in Petite-Bourgogne, performed in the neighbourhood several times throughout his childhood. In a park that had a public piano, Jason once shared the keyboard with the famous musician during a summer camp. He was nine years old. He played with him again a few years later. Jason’s face lights up even more when he learns that the 87-year-old jazz legend is one of the guests of honour at the round table held as part of the festival. Another legend, Ethel Bruneau, the queen of tap dance, is now 86.
Au Centre culturel Georges-Vanier, à deu: At the Centre culturel Georges-Vanier, a stone’s throw from where Mr. Jones grew up, and in the neighbourhood where Ms. Bruneau lived when she arrived in Montréal, the veterans tell an attentive audience their story, punctuated with previously untold anecdotes, and that of the communities that lived in the neighbourhood. Panellists Michael Farkas, who for 15 years has led Youth in Motion, an organization dedicated to young people in Petite-Bourgogne, and jazz musician Modibo Keita, a Saint-Henri resident, share their perspectives in an intergenerational conversation.
À la toute fin, Jason souhaite poser une: At the very end, Jason wants to ask a question. At the microphone, he explains who he is. “Mr. Jones, in the past, I played with you twice. You might not recognize me, but I’m a big fan. I was wondering if there was a way to keep the legacy of jazz alive here.” As he approaches, Oliver Jones recognizes the young musician, who has changed a lot since they met.
Il lui serre la main sous les applaudiss: He shakes his hand to applause. “Congratulations! You can’t give up.” “Never!” answers Jason. “It’s so important. I’ve always told my students to never stop. There’s no such thing as bad music. And I’m sure you’ll make it.”
Jason Magellan, et les légendaires Olive: Jason Magellan, and the legendary Oliver Jones and Ethel Bruneau. Photo: Pierre Langlois
Pour la saxophoniste new-yorkaise Nicole: For New York saxophonist Nicole Glover, something is being confirmed. “The community is really integrated, whether in the concerts, the master classes, the listening sessions, the outdoor events. I feel like I’ve really seen the community over the past two days, and that’s what I appreciate,” says the 30-year-old musician. In this respect, the atmosphere differs from what is sometimes seen elsewhere. “I feel like the festival really understands what’s important, which is good music and a sense of community. At some festivals, the priorities are sometimes different,” notes the musician, who has performed abroad.
Si cette dernière s’est intéressée au ja: Although she was drawn to jazz from a young age, it was through community programs that she was able to hone her skills as a teenager, before heading to university. “I got to meet people who were interested in music like me, which was very formative.
Avant, je voyais toujours la musique que: Before, I always saw the music I played as something outdated that no longer existed,” says Ms. Glover, who discovered a living scene as a result. “It strengthened my desire to keep playing music.”
Nicole Glover, saxophoniste, donne un at: Nicole Glover, saxophonist, leads a workshop. Photo: Pierre Langlois
Elle ajoute que, aux États-Unis, où elle: She adds that in the United States, where she grew up, the vast majority of these programs, some local, others national, are not government-funded. “Most often it’s a private or non-profit venture. They’re people who are willing to teach and organize, and students who are willing to come,” she says.
Cependant, il y existe une culture du ja: There, however, a strong jazz culture exists, no doubt because this music was born on American soil. Pianist Taurey Butler has lived in Montréal for 12 years. He accompanied Nicole Butler on piano during these performances. “They’re visionaries,” he says of the organization. “There are two things: the integration of the community, but they also bring musicians together. I feel like that’s something that was missing in my field,” says the musician during the jam. There is no place where musicians can get together. In New Jersey, where he grew up, Mr. Butler studied piano in high school.
« Certains d’entre nous se réunissaient: “Some of us would get together to play,” he recalls. “Otherwise, I learned on my own, by taking part in jams,” says the musician, who studied engineering and languages at university. “I’m proof that you don’t need to study music at university. It can help, but if you have the passion, you can develop it yourself,” he adds. He recommends having teachers or some form of coaching to be well guided.
Taurey Butler, pianiste, sur scène. Phot: Taurey Butler, pianist, on stage. Photo: Chris Maskell
Traditionnellement, c’est de cette façon: Traditionally, this is how musicians learned to play jazz: novices learned from their elders. “In the past, people learned by joining a band and doing an apprenticeship,” explains Sam Kirmayer, co-founder of the Société de Jazz de Saint-Henri. Everything changed in the 1990s with the arrival of jazz programs in universities. “People learned by going to school, and schools haven’t been very proactive about breaking down barriers,” he says. Valérie Lacombe agrees.
Voilà pourquoi elle favorise le mentorat: That is why she favours mentorship and community practice over the school environment. “We imported the European way of doing things: the programs are based on classical music, whereas jazz is more of an oral tradition, passed down, where you receive knowledge orally, for example in a jazz club,” she explains. “These institutions are white men’s institutions, and the programs aren’t designed to showcase the Black culture in which jazz evolved,” laments the drummer, who studied at McGill.
C’est dans cette perspective que la SJSH: It is in this spirit that the SJSH wants to move forward.
